subject: pk modeling in stan: one compartmental model with lag

messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: pk modeling in stan: one compartmental model with lag
parts:
Hi,

Does anybody have experience with modeling a lag?  Technically the first derivative is discontinuous at lag time and the model as it is described in textbooks doesn't converge in stan. 

Thanks for any advice,
Linas

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: pk modeling in stan: one compartmental model with lag
parts:
Hi!

Stan does not care to my knowledge about the discontinuity in the derivative - rather the discontinuity in the log-likelihood is a problem. However, if the data is such that Stan will not often try out parameter values which cause these jumps in the log-lik, then it is ok.

I did fit lag time models (in simple PK settings) and I was surprised how well it worked - but I can't recall if I had so much courage to put a random effect on the tlag; probably not.

In short: just try it... otherwise you can always us the transit cmt approach.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: pk modeling in stan: one compartmental model with lag
parts:
Hi!

I would put the random effect on the parameter where I think it is needed more likely or if I have no idea about that put it on the parameter where I want minimal bias on the pop mean.

Concerning your model: I don´t see the tlag, i.e. there must be a step function somewhere, I think. Also: Are you sure about the additive noise on the natural scale? I always go for log-normal residual error if possible. Moreover: You know the order of the terms such that you have no problem in calculating the expression in log-space which is what I would always advise to do (you anyway sample log-parameters).

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: pk modeling in stan: one compartmental model with lag
parts:
Hi!

There are pros and cons for any of the choices - this is my opinion: From my experience it is always good (numerical wise) to fit ke; or since we are fitting the logs of it, I prefer to fit 1/ke which is the mean residence time; something I understand much better and can hence give better priors. On the contrary, the allometic weight scaling theory stuff is only applicable to Cl and V. Now, what I tend to do, is fit MRTs and then convert them to Cl, apply allometric scaling to Cl and V to finally calculate the patient specific MRT_j. Handling rates or MRTs is a matter of sign-convention on the log-scale...

In principle, I think, you want random effects on all parameters. It usually a compromise of what you can fit with your data and how willing you are to use informative priors on the omegas (variance components of the random effects). Again, this is also a very specific question which can only be answered in the context of your problem and data.

My last point concerning logs: I always calculate the log of the concentrations, so I tend to use the log_diff_exp() / log_sum_exp() functions very often. If you keep all the computations in log space, then all those products become just sums (should be easier for Stan to deal with). The concentration 0 I then always represent as -25, which is reasonably close to 0 on the natural scale.

Best,
Sebastian

parts:
Hi,

Thanks a lot for your comments.

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: pk modeling in stan: one compartmental model with lag
parts:
It looks like ka, cl, ke & tlag are performing best, i.e. with this parametrization you end up having the least correlations, but you are certainly right that in this problem it may not really matter what you take - again this depends on your data which I just don´t know. Interpreting the mean and the sd makes more sense on the logarithmic scale in this case. However, if a time unit of 1 is a meaningful change, then putting a random effect on ka seems to have little to no effect on the results.

Sebastian

PS: My recommendations are of course the result of my data and my models (2-cmt oral) I work with at the moment.
